title: Developmental malformation of the corpus callosum: a review of typical callosal development and examples of developmental disorders with callosal involvement

subsections.section_title: Typical Development, Anatomy, and Organization of the Corpus Callosum
subsections.subsection_title: Prenatal Development and Formation of the Corpus Callosum
subsections.content:
Prenatal formation of the corpus callosum is a staged process that depends on prior remodeling of the rostral telencephalic midline rather than simple late crossing of neocortical axons. Classical human embryological studies localized the future callosal pathway to the dorsal lamina reuniens/hippocampal primordium, where infolding, apposition, and fusion of the midline establish a commissural substrate; the cavum septi pellucidi subsequently emerges as a transient pocket beneath the growing anterior callosal border and is later sealed by rostral development ref [2]. This framework remains influential because it links callosal morphogenesis to neighboring septal and hippocampal development rather than to an isolated white-matter event ref [2].

Modern fetal imaging and histological studies refine the timing of these events. Diffusion tensor MRI of second-trimester specimens shows that major commissural tracts are not equally timed: the anterior commissure and optic chiasm are already evident when the corpus callosum is still absent, whereas callosal fibers become clearly identifiable around 14-15 gestational weeks and then expand in both anterior and posterior directions through the later second trimester ref [1], ref [3]. These data also indicate rapid concomitant growth of the hippocampal commissure and progressive callosal extension toward the future splenium, consistent with earlier anatomical observations ref [1], ref [2], ref [3].

Importantly, prenatal callosal formation in humans appears to rely on conserved cellular and molecular guidance systems. Combined anatomical, immunohistochemical, and DTI analyses demonstrate the presence of midline zipper glia, glial wedge, indusium griseum glia, subcallosal sling-like populations, and cingulate pioneering axons in the 13-20 week human fetal brain, alongside expression of guidance and regulatory molecules including SLIT/ROBO, NETRIN1/DCC, NFIA, EMX1, and GAP43 ref [3]. Thus, typical prenatal callosal development is best understood as the coordinated outcome of midline fusion, transient glial scaffolding, pioneer axon formation, and regionally ordered ingrowth of commissural fibers; disruption at any of these steps provides a developmental basis for callosal dysgenesis and agenesis ref [2], ref [3].

subsections.section_title: Typical Development, Anatomy, and Organization of the Corpus Callosum
subsections.subsection_title: Gross Anatomy and Regional Topography
subsections.content:
Grossly, the corpus callosum is the largest cerebral commissure and is conventionally divided on the midsagittal view into the rostrum, genu, body (trunk), isthmus, and splenium. This macroscopic partition is not merely descriptive: lesion-based human mapping showed a reproducible anterior–posterior topography in which inferior frontal and anterior inferior parietal interhemispheric fibers traverse the rostrum and genu, whereas posterior association and visual projections are concentrated more caudally, especially within the splenium ref [4].

Regional topography is therefore only partly captured by simple geometric subdivision. In the human material analyzed by de Lacoste and colleagues, fibers from the temporo-parieto-occipital junction coursed through the caudal body and splenium, while superior parietal and occipital cortices projected almost exclusively through the splenium; by contrast, no clear callosal degeneration followed lesions in the anterior superior frontal region, suggesting relative regional sparsity or atypical organization of callosal connectivity there ref [4]. These observations broadly align with classical primate data while underscoring species-specific displacement of frontal projections toward more rostral callosal sectors in humans ref [2], ref [3].

An important gross-anatomical principle is that visible callosal segments do not correspond one-to-one with lobar boundaries; rather, each segment contains intermixed but biased bundles whose arrangement reflects cortical geography and evolutionary expansion of association cortex. Accordingly, the genu and anterior body are typically linked to frontal interhemispheric transfer, the midbody to sensorimotor and parietal territories, and the isthmus-splenium complex to posterior parietal, temporal, and occipital cortices, providing the macroscopic framework used to interpret developmental malformations and their clinicoradiologic correlates ref [4], ref [3], ref [4].

subsections.section_title: Typical Development, Anatomy, and Organization of the Corpus Callosum
subsections.subsection_title: Structural and Functional Fiber Organization
subsections.content:
Beyond gross topography, the corpus callosum is organized as a set of partially segregated but overlapping interhemispheric channels whose microstructural properties constrain functional coupling. Diffusion tractography combined with functional localization has shown that callosal motor fibers connecting primary motor cortices occupy the posterior body and isthmus and display a somatotopic arrangement, with hand fibers positioned relatively anterior and ventral to foot fibers; importantly, fractional anisotropy within these hand-related callosal fibers correlates with transcallosal interhemispheric inhibition, directly linking local microstructure to physiological efficacy of interhemispheric communication ref [5]. This supports the broader view that callosal organization is not purely geometric, but reflects connectional architecture and systems-specific conduction demands.

Comparable principles are evident in posterior callosal systems. In the splenium, occipital-callosal tracts can be functionally subdivided by the visual field maps associated with their cortical endpoints: dorsal extrastriate and parietal-occipital visual regions project through a broad middle band of the splenium, whereas ventral visual regions traverse its inferior-anterior sector ref [6]. These data further suggest a coarse eccentricity-related ordering within dorsal occipital callosal fibers, indicating that the callosum preserves aspects of cortical functional layout rather than simply bundling fibers by lobe of origin ref [6].

At the same time, tractography studies also reveal an important caveat for interpreting typical organization: sensitivity is uneven across systems. Both motor and occipital analyses indicate reliable localization of major commissural bundles, yet fibers traversing regions of crossing or sharp curvature are more likely to be underdetected, particularly for lateral and ventral cortical projections ref [5], ref [6]. Thus, current descriptions of structural-functional organization should be understood as robust maps of the dominant callosal pathways, while acknowledging that finer-scale interdigitation and weaker projections are likely underestimated.

subsections.section_title: Typical Development, Anatomy, and Organization of the Corpus Callosum
subsections.subsection_title: Clinical and Developmental Variants Informing Typical Organization
subsections.content:
Clinical and developmental variants provide a powerful natural experiment for inferring typical callosal organization. In malformed brains, the pattern of callosal absence, hypoplasia, or atrophy often covaries with the timing and topography of broader cerebral disturbance, helping distinguish primary dysgenesis from secondary loss. Early MRI work showed that callosal anomalies are frequent in congenital brain malformations and are highly informative about associated anomalies and developmental timing, whereas a complete but thinned corpus callosum more often suggests later cortical or white-matter injury rather than failed commissuration ref [7].

Lesion-based developmental studies further support a stable anteroposterior cortical-callosal map. In children with pre- or perinatal focal injury, regional thinning of the corpus callosum tracks lesion location: anterior reductions correspond to frontal damage, midbody changes to perirolandic regions, and posterior/splenial reductions to parietal-occipital injury, closely matching primate and adult human topographies ref [8]. Likewise, tractography-based segmentation in young children with developmental delay showed globally smaller callosal areas and, importantly, a weakened correspondence between callosal subregions and the white-matter volumes of their presumed cortical targets, implying disruption of the normal scaling relation between cortex and commissural output ref [10].

Callosal dysgenesis also reveals which organizational principles are preserved despite major malformation. Diffusion tractography demonstrates that residual or hypoplastic callosal fibers often retain broadly normal topography, while uncrossed fibers may form Probst bundles and other aberrant tracts, indicating both developmental constraint and plastic re-routing ref [9]. Together, these variants show that typical callosal organization reflects a robust regional blueprint, but one whose final caliber and connectivity remain sensitive to developmental timing, cortical target integrity, and compensatory reorganization ref [7], ref [8], ref [9], ref [10].

subsections.section_title: Morphometric, Microstructural, and Functional Characterization
subsections.subsection_title: Developmental Morphology and Callosal Formation
subsections.content:
Normal callosal morphogenesis begins with fusion of the telencephalic midline and establishment of the commissural plate, followed by the first transmidline axons at approximately 12–14 postconceptional weeks and rapid expansion of the callosal plate thereafter ref [3]. Classical embryologic observations and modern fetal MRI/DTI together indicate that early growth proceeds in an anteroposterior sequence, with the rostral body and genu recognized before later maturation of posterior callosal regions ref [3].

A central advance from human developmental studies is the demonstration that the canonical midline guidance apparatus described in rodents is also present in the fetal human brain. Histological and molecular analyses identified the glial wedge, indusium griseum glia, midline zipper glia, and a subcallosal sling-like population, together with cingulate pioneering axons and expression of guidance-related molecules including Netrin1, Slit/Robo components, NFIA, EMX1, and neuropilin-1 ref [3]. These findings support substantial conservation of the cellular and molecular logic of commissural crossing across species ref [3].

Later fetal expansion of the corpus callosum is not simply a matter of fiber accretion. Human-specific transient morphogenetic zones become prominent between roughly 20 and 45 postconceptional weeks, notably callosal septa and the subcallosal zone, which create modular and laminar 'grooves' along the ventral callosal tier ref [11]. These structures are enriched in extracellular matrix, GFAP-positive elements, neurons, and semaphorin-3A-related signaling, and are thought to scaffold continued bundle growth, topographic ordering, and possibly subsequent remodeling as exuberant interhemispheric projections are refined in late gestation and early postnatal life ref [11].

subsections.section_title: Morphometric, Microstructural, and Functional Characterization
subsections.subsection_title: Diffusion MRI and Tractography Methods for Callosal Microstructure
subsections.content:
Diffusion MRI has become the principal in vivo approach for probing callosal microstructure because the corpus callosum combines high anisotropy with a relatively coherent commissural geometry. Early diffusion tensor tractography formalized streamline reconstruction from the principal eigenvector field and demonstrated anatomically plausible trajectories through the splenium and callosal body, while also making explicit the dependence of tracking on smoothing, step size, anisotropy thresholds, and noise control ref [12]. Quantitative tensor measures such as fractional anisotropy, mean diffusivity, axial diffusivity, and radial diffusivity are now routinely used as indirect markers of axonal packing, coherence, and myelination, although they remain nonspecific to underlying histology.

A key methodological limitation is that the tensor model is voxel-averaged and performs poorly in regions of fiber complexity. Work on intravoxel crossing and planar diffusion showed that even near callosal projections, intersections with corona radiata or other association systems can lower anisotropy and bias principal-direction estimates, thereby complicating tractography-based inference about callosal continuity ref [13]. These issues motivated more advanced approaches, including high-angular-resolution diffusion imaging, q-ball imaging, constrained spherical deconvolution, and probabilistic tractography, which better accommodate crossing, fanning, and uncertainty while improving delineation of callosal subcomponents.

For developmental and malformation studies, tractography is especially valuable when combined with midsagittal morphology. Fiber-based segmentation of the corpus callosum into lobar projection zones provides a more anatomically grounded alternative to geometric partition schemes and can reveal altered structure-function scaling in atypical development ref [10]. In young children with developmental delay, tractography-derived callosal subdivisions were globally reduced and, importantly, their usual correlations with corresponding cortical white-matter volumes were diminished ref [10]. Accordingly, diffusion MRI in callosal disorders is most informative when interpreted jointly across acquisition quality, reconstruction model, tractography strategy, and anatomically constrained segmentation.

subsections.section_title: Morphometric, Microstructural, and Functional Characterization
subsections.subsection_title: Topography, Microstructure, and Cognitive-Motor Function
subsections.content:
Callosal topography is functionally organized rather than adequately captured by gross geometric partitioning alone. Tractography studies have refined this view by showing that motor callosal fibers occupy the posterior body/isthmus and are somatotopically arranged, with hand fibers located relatively anterior and ventral to foot fibers, while broader parcellation schemes identify distinct temporal, parietal, occipital, and frontal projection zones across the midsagittal callosum ref [5], ref [4], ref [5]. This topographic precision is especially relevant for developmental disorders with callosal involvement, where region-specific compromise may differentially affect language, sensorimotor integration, and higher cognition.

A consistent theme across diffusion MRI studies is that microstructural indices of the corpus callosum covary with domain-specific performance. In the motor system, fractional anisotropy (FA) of hand callosal motor fibers correlates with transcallosal interhemispheric inhibition, directly linking tract microstructure to functional connectivity ref [5]. More globally, reduced callosal integrity has been associated with slower interhemispheric processing on crossed-uncrossed and redundant-target paradigms, indicating that altered FA and diffusivity can influence the efficiency of sensorimotor transfer rather than merely reflect anatomic variation ref [15]. Related work further shows that callosal integrity predicts bimanual coordination skills, supporting the behavioral relevance of regional callosal organization ref [6].

These structure-function relationships extend beyond motor behavior into developing language networks. In children, diffusivity within temporal-callosal pathways predicts phonological awareness and related reading measures, suggesting that posterior callosal microstructure contributes to the maturation of interhemispheric language processing ref [14]. Together, such findings argue that in corpus callosum malformations, cognitive-motor outcome depends not only on the presence or size of the commissure, but on which topographic sectors form, how coherent their microstructure is, and whether residual or ectopic pathways can sustain efficient interhemispheric communication ref [5], ref [14], ref [15].

subsections.section_title: Morphometric, Microstructural, and Functional Characterization
subsections.subsection_title: Interhemispheric Transfer and Functional Dynamics Across the Lifespan
subsections.content:
Interhemispheric transfer is not static across development, but reflects changing balances among callosal myelination, computational demand, and the efficiency of alternative commissural or subcortical routes. A life-span framework emphasizes that childhood is marked by improving transfer speed and integration, whereas later adulthood may show greater reliance on bilateral recruitment as single-hemisphere processing resources decline rather than a simple loss of lateralization ref [17]. In typically developing children, behavioral and electrophysiological indices converge on progressive improvement in interhemispheric interaction from late childhood into adolescence, consistent with ongoing functional maturation of the corpus callosum ref [16], ref [17].

Classic paradigms quantify these dynamics with crossed-uncrossed reaction time differences, bilateral field advantage, and evoked-potential interhemispheric transmission time. In normal development, bilateral field advantage for visual matching increases with age, while evoked-potential transmission time tends to shorten, supporting the idea that maturational gains in myelination have measurable behavioral consequences ref [16]. More broadly, reaction-time studies indicate that the small crossed-uncrossed difference in healthy individuals is compatible with rapid callosal transfer, whereas much larger delays after commissurotomy and intermediate effects in callosal agenesis reveal recruitment of slower noncallosal pathways ref [18]. These findings are directly relevant to developmental malformations, where preserved performance may mask qualitatively different routing of information between hemispheres.

Across the lifespan, functional outcome depends not only on whether information can cross hemispheres, but also on task complexity and channel capacity. Banich and Brown argue that interhemispheric cooperation is advantageous when unilateral resources are taxed, but imposes communication overhead for simpler operations ref [17]. This principle helps explain why children with immature callosal systems, individuals with agenesis of the corpus callosum, and older adults can show different patterns of bilateral benefit depending on perceptual or cognitive load ref [17], ref [18]. For developmental callosal disorders, therefore, functional assessment should move beyond gross transfer success toward age-sensitive measures of timing, efficiency, and compensatory network organization.

subsections.section_title: Congenital and Genetic Disorders with Callosal Involvement
subsections.subsection_title: Neurofibromatosis Type 1 and Callosal White Matter Abnormalities
subsections.content:
Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) is a common autosomal-dominant disorder with frequent central nervous system involvement and a well-recognized burden of cognitive and behavioral morbidity, making it a relevant model of genetically mediated callosal white-matter alteration ref [8], ref [21]. Conventional MRI studies first emphasized the high prevalence of T2-hyperintense "unidentified bright objects" and the broader tendency toward abnormal white-matter development in NF1, findings not limited to focal lesions but extending to diffuse alterations in brain growth and organization ref [22], ref [19].

With respect to the corpus callosum, morphometric studies in children with NF1 consistently report enlargement rather than simple hypoplasia. In a family-controlled volumetric study, Greenwood et al. found significantly increased total cerebral white-matter volume and a larger midsagittal callosal area, with white-matter expansion especially prominent in frontal regions ref [19]. Similarly, Kayl et al. showed larger total callosal area and enlargement of the rostral body and midbody in children with NF1, including those with comorbid attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder ref [20]. These observations suggest that callosal involvement in NF1 more often reflects dysregulated white-matter overgrowth or aberrant maturation than classic agenetic malformation ref [19], ref [20].

Microstructural imaging further indicates that gross enlargement does not imply normal connectivity. Diffusion tensor MRI in adults with NF1 demonstrated cerebral microstructural abnormalities consistent with altered white-matter integrity, supporting the view that callosal size changes may coexist with abnormal fiber organization ref [23]. Clinically, these white-matter and callosal abnormalities likely contribute to the heterogeneous NF1 cognitive phenotype, which includes reduced IQ, visuospatial deficits, executive dysfunction, and attention problems ref [21], ref [19], ref [20]. Importantly, associations between T2 hyperintensities and cognition or morphology remain inconsistent across studies, underscoring that diffuse developmental dysmyelination or altered axonal organization may be more informative than lesion counts alone ref [19], ref [21], ref [22].

subsections.section_title: Congenital and Genetic Disorders with Callosal Involvement
subsections.subsection_title: 22q11.2 Deletion Syndrome and Midline White Matter Development
subsections.content:
22q11.2 deletion syndrome (22q11.2DS; velocardiofacial/DiGeorge syndrome) is notable for recurrent abnormalities of midline brain development, making it highly relevant to disorders of callosal formation and interhemispheric connectivity. Early quantitative MRI studies in adults and children described reduced total and regional white matter, increased rates of cavum septum pellucidum, and abnormalities involving the corpus callosum and adjacent midline structures, suggesting that disturbed hemispheric integration is a core neurodevelopmental feature rather than an incidental finding [ref 1], [ref 2], [ref 3], [ref 4].

Diffusion imaging strengthened this interpretation by showing that white matter disruption extends beyond gross volumetry. Barnea-Goraly et al. reported reduced fractional anisotropy in frontal, parietal, and temporal association pathways in VCFS, with altered frontotemporal connectivity and atypical signal in posterior callosal regions [ref 5]. Subsequent pediatric DTI/VBM work confirmed widespread microstructural abnormalities in interhemispheric and midline tracts, including the splenium and body of the corpus callosum, cingulum, internal capsule, and superior corona radiata, even when volumetric findings were partly dissociable from FA changes [ref 6]. Complementing these tract-based observations, corpus callosum morphometry studies documented altered size and shape, including posterior displacement and regional dysmorphology, in affected children [ref 3], [ref 7], [ref 8].

Cortical mapping studies further indicate that midline disturbance in 22q11.2DS is not confined to the callosum itself. Children with the deletion show thinning in anterior cingulate, medial frontal, posterior cingulate, and ventromedial occipito-temporal cortices, together with abnormal occipital gyrification, implicating aberrant development of medial cortical territories that normally contribute callosal projection systems and higher-order integration [ref 9]. Taken together, the 22q11.2DS literature supports a model of abnormal midline patterning in which callosal morphology, neighboring septal structures, medial cortex, and long-range white matter maturation are jointly affected [ref 1], [ref 5], [ref 6], [ref 9].

subsections.section_title: Congenital and Genetic Disorders with Callosal Involvement
subsections.subsection_title: Agenesis and Dysgenesis of the Corpus Callosum
subsections.content:
Agenesis and dysgenesis of the corpus callosum (ACC/CCD) comprise a heterogeneous spectrum that includes complete or partial agenesis and hypoplasia, often reflecting broader disturbances of forebrain development rather than an isolated commissural defect. Population-based data indicate that ACC and hypoplasia diagnosed in infancy occur at a combined prevalence of about 1.8 per 10,000 live births, with frequent associations with chromosomal, somatic, and additional CNS malformations ref [28]. MRI series similarly emphasize that apparently “isolated” cases are uncommon in clinically ascertained cohorts, with frequent cortical malformations, reduced hemispheric white matter volume, abnormal anterior or hippocampal commissures, and posterior fossa anomalies ref [30], ref [8].

Prognosis is therefore strongly shaped by lesion type and by associated abnormalities. Prenatal cohorts suggest that partial and isolated forms generally have better outcomes than complete ACC, whereas associated CNS anomalies and chromosomal disorders markedly worsen developmental prognosis ref [29]. In clinical series, only a minority of children achieve normal or near-normal development, and poorer outcome is associated with microcephaly, epilepsy, cerebral palsy, and concomitant cerebral dysgenesis ref [8]. Even among individuals with normal-range intelligence, more subtle impairments in higher-order reasoning, social cognition, and psychosocial functioning are well documented ref [12].

Neuroimaging and tractography further show that CCD is not simply absence of a commissure, but a reorganization of long-range connectivity. Hypoplastic callosa may preserve coarse topography, whereas agenesis commonly yields Probst bundles and other aberrant pathways, illustrating substantial developmental plasticity despite atypical interhemispheric wiring ref [10]. Hypoplasia itself is clinically important rather than incidental, occurring with a frequency comparable to complete and partial agenesis in pediatric MRI series and associating with developmental impairment ref [11]. Overall, ACC/CCD should be viewed as a neurodevelopmental connectivity disorder whose outcome depends on the extent of associated brain malformation and compensatory reorganization ref [30], ref [10].

subsections.section_title: Congenital and Genetic Disorders with Callosal Involvement
subsections.subsection_title: Other Genetic Syndromes with Callosal Morphology Changes
subsections.content:
Beyond classic agenesis/dysgenesis phenotypes, several genetic syndromes show more circumscribed callosal remodeling. Williams syndrome is the best-characterized example in this category. Structural MRI studies consistently describe an abnormally shaped corpus callosum, with reduced midsagittal length, altered curvature, and preferential involvement of posterior callosal regions rather than complete absence of commissural tissue ref [37], ref [8], ref [9].

In Williams syndrome, quantitative morphometry has shown a smaller overall callosal volume after adjustment for brain size, with the most reproducible reductions in the caudal body, isthmus, and especially splenium ref [8], ref [9]. Higher-resolution surface-based analyses further indicate that the callosum is shorter and less curved, with focal thinning distributed across the posterior profile and persisting, though in a more restricted form, after scaling for total brain size ref [37]. This posterior emphasis is notable given the broader parieto-occipital and dorsal-stream abnormalities repeatedly reported in the syndrome ref [6], ref [9].

These callosal changes are therefore interpreted less as a primary failure of commissural formation than as part of a syndrome-specific alteration in interhemispheric white-matter development and cortical patterning. Reviews of the Williams syndrome neuroanatomical phenotype place callosal abnormalities alongside reduced cerebral white matter, atypical gyrification, altered hemispheric shape, and posterior cortical anomalies, supporting the view that subtle callosal morphology can serve as a marker of abnormal midline and association-system development in multisystem genetic disorders ref [6], ref [8].

subsections.section_title: Congenital and Genetic Disorders with Callosal Involvement
subsections.subsection_title: Sex Chromosome Disorders: Turner Syndrome with Callosal Involvement
subsections.content:
Turner syndrome provides an informative model for sex-chromosome effects on midline brain development. Although gross callosal malformations are uncommon, several case reports have documented complete agenesis of the corpus callosum in individuals with monosomy X or related karyotypes, including classic 45,X Turner syndrome and ring-X mosaicism, often accompanied by additional systemic anomalies and variable cognitive impairment ref [38], ref [39], ref [40]. These observations suggest that, while agenesis is rare, callosal development can be disrupted in a subset of patients with Turner syndrome.

Beyond these rare malformations, quantitative MRI studies indicate subtler but reproducible callosal and associated white-matter changes. In a volumetric study of girls with X monosomy, overall cerebral size was not significantly reduced, but regional tissue distribution was altered, with bilateral parietal reductions and a right-sided predominance of abnormalities, paralleling visuospatial and attentional deficits ref [6]. A subsequent midsagittal morphometric study found a distinct pattern of midline involvement, including reduced area of the corpus callosum genu together with posterior fossa abnormalities, notably reduced pons and vermis VI-VII areas and enlargement of the fourth ventricle ref [15].

Collectively, the Turner syndrome literature supports a spectrum of callosal involvement ranging from complete agenesis in isolated case reports to more subtle dysmorphology affecting interhemispheric connectivity, especially in networks linked to parietal and frontoparietal function ref [38], ref [40], ref [6], ref [15]. These findings are consistent with the broader view that altered X-chromosome dosage, and possibly interactions with hormonal milieu, can influence midline white-matter patterning during development ref [6], ref [15].

subsections.section_title: Prenatal and Neurodevelopmental Risk Factors Affecting Callosal Development
subsections.subsection_title: Prenatal Alcohol Exposure and Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorders
subsections.content:
Prenatal alcohol exposure is among the best-documented environmental teratogens affecting corpus callosum development. Early neuropathological reports described complete or partial agenesis, thinning, and broader midline dysgenesis in severe fetal alcohol syndrome (FAS), implicating alcohol exposure during critical periods of commissural formation ref [45]. MRI studies in surviving children extended these observations, showing that callosal involvement is not limited to rare agenesis: alcohol-exposed cohorts exhibit reduced midsagittal callosal area, with disproportionate reduction in anterior and posterior sectors even after accounting for smaller overall brain size ref [44], ref [45].

Subsequent morphometric and diffusion studies reinforced the view that posterior callosal regions may be especially vulnerable. Shape analyses and quantitative mapping linked heavy prenatal alcohol exposure to thinning and displacement of posterior callosal segments ref [7], while DTI studies identified reduced fractional anisotropy and other microstructural abnormalities in the isthmus and splenium, extending from the midline into interhemispheric white matter pathways ref [47], ref [6], ref [8]. These findings fit with broader evidence of altered white matter organization in fetal alcohol spectrum disorders (FASD), including splenial abnormalities associated with reduced white matter integrity ref [47].

Importantly, callosal abnormalities in FASD have functional correlates. Poorer bimanual coordination and less accurate performance on tasks that increasingly depend on interhemispheric interaction have been related to callosal compromise in alcohol-exposed children ref [46]. Similarly, interhemispheric tactile transfer deficits and visuomotor integration problems correlate with callosal or splenial abnormalities ref [46], ref [47], ref [9]. Although severity varies across the FASD spectrum and is not fully explained by facial dysmorphology alone ref [6], the convergent structural and behavioral literature supports the corpus callosum as a major target of prenatal alcohol-related neurodevelopmental injury ref [44], ref [45].

subsections.section_title: Prenatal and Neurodevelopmental Risk Factors Affecting Callosal Development
subsections.subsection_title: Prematurity and Perinatal White Matter Injury
subsections.content:
Premature birth exposes the developing corpus callosum to a period of exceptional vulnerability, when axonal organization, pre-oligodendrocyte maturation, and early myelination are still incomplete. Serial diffusion tensor imaging has shown that, in healthy preterm maturation, diffusivity normally declines and anisotropy increases across late gestation, whereas infants with white matter injury fail to show these maturational trajectories in widespread regions, including the corpus callosum and frontal white matter ref [49]. Longitudinal MRI studies further indicate that diffuse white matter abnormalities and ventricular dilation are common by term-equivalent age in extremely preterm infants, underscoring that callosal compromise often arises as part of a broader encephalopathy of prematurity rather than an isolated commissural lesion ref [14].

Morphometric studies consistently report impaired callosal growth after very preterm birth. Cranial ultrasound measurements suggest that callosal length grows at roughly half the expected in utero rate after preterm delivery, with reduced growth detectable by 6 weeks in most infants and particularly poor growth between 2 and 6 weeks relating to later psychomotor delay and cerebral palsy ref [9], ref [13]. By adolescence, very preterm survivors show smaller midsagittal callosal area, especially in posterior and mid-posterior sectors adjacent to the periventricular region, and the greatest reductions are seen in those with prior periventricular hemorrhage and ventricular dilatation ref [52].

Microstructural studies help explain these volumetric findings. In preterm infants with diffuse excessive high signal intensity at term-equivalent age, radial diffusivity is elevated in the splenium, with broader increases in axial and radial diffusivity across cerebral white matter, consistent with widespread oligodendroglial and/or axonal disturbance ref [11]. Functional consequences also persist: young adults with perinatal callosal damage show altered fMRI activation during auditory and visual tasks requiring interhemispheric transfer, suggesting compensatory reorganization rather than normal callosal processing ref [8]. Together, these data position prematurity-related white matter injury as a major acquired pathway to callosal hypoplasia, dysmaturation, and long-term deficits in interhemispheric integration ref [49], ref [52], ref [8].

subsections.section_title: Prenatal and Neurodevelopmental Risk Factors Affecting Callosal Development
subsections.subsection_title: ADHD, Autism, and Other Neurodevelopmental Conditions
subsections.content:
Callosal development is also perturbed in common neurodevelopmental disorders that do not typically present with overt callosal malformations. In ADHD, structural findings have been heterogeneous at the single-study level, but meta-analytic synthesis indicates modest and regionally selective reductions, particularly in the splenium, with some evidence for sex-related variation and additional involvement of more anterior sectors in boys ref [56]. Functional studies further suggest that these morphometric differences are accompanied by altered interhemispheric transfer, with atypical directionality and subtype-specific effects in adults with inattentive versus combined ADHD, implying that callosal anomalies in ADHD may reflect both altered maturation and altered physiological efficiency of interhemispheric communication ref [60].

Autism spectrum disorder has provided some of the most consistent evidence for callosal involvement. Early MRI studies reported reduced overall or regional callosal size, although the implicated segments differed somewhat across cohorts and parcellation schemes: posterior reductions were emphasized in some samples, whereas others found greater involvement of anterior regions, especially the genu and rostrum ref [16], ref [15], ref [9]. Despite this variability, the broad pattern points to reduced interhemispheric connectivity rather than complete absence of commissural formation. Diffusion tensor imaging extended these observations by showing lower fractional anisotropy in and near the corpus callosum across childhood to adulthood, indicating that atypical microstructural organization persists beyond early development ref [10].

More broadly, these findings support the view that callosal abnormalities in neurodevelopmental conditions often index altered network formation rather than isolated midline defects. In ADHD and autism alike, callosal changes are plausibly linked to disturbed long-range integration among frontal, parietal, temporal, and occipital association systems, and may contribute to deficits in attention, executive control, social cognition, and multisensory integration ref [56], ref [60], ref [10]. Thus, within this risk-factor framework, the corpus callosum can be viewed as a sensitive marker of atypical developmental timing, axonal organization, and interhemispheric specialization across a range of neurodevelopmental phenotypes ref [9], ref [15], ref [16].

subsections.section_title: Prenatal and Neurodevelopmental Risk Factors Affecting Callosal Development
subsections.subsection_title: Language, Reading, and Neurodevelopmental Disorders
subsections.content:
Language and reading disorders provide an important example of neurodevelopmental conditions in which callosal variation may index altered interhemispheric integration rather than a primary commissural malformation. Clinical reviews of developmental language disorder emphasize its heterogeneity, spanning mixed receptive-expressive, expressive, and higher-order semantic-pragmatic phenotypes, and note that routine structural lesions are uncommon despite clear developmental impairment ref [64]. Longitudinal work further shows that persistent preschool language impairment, especially deficits in syntax and comprehension, predicts later literacy difficulties, whereas isolated early phonological delay is less strongly related to reading outcome ref [14].

Within this framework, several imaging studies have linked reading and oral-language profiles to callosal anatomy. Leonard et al. reported that neuroanatomical variation predicts distinct language and reading phenotypes, with children showing broader comprehension deficits occupying a different anatomical profile from those with more selective decoding problems ref [14]. Earlier MRI work in dyslexia also identified atypical posterior hemispheric asymmetry and a relatively larger splenium, implicating altered interhemispheric organization in temporo-parietal language networks ref [17]. Family-based MRI data similarly associated individual differences in oral reading with midsagittal callosal area, particularly the midbody, even after adjustment for whole-brain volume, IQ, and gender ref [18].

Diffusion imaging has refined these observations by showing that microstructure of callosal pathways is related to phonological skill. In children, diffusivity within temporal-callosal fibers predicts phonological awareness, word attack, and passage comprehension, highlighting the relevance of interhemispheric temporal lobe connectivity for reading acquisition ref [16]. Collectively, these findings suggest that callosal involvement in language and reading disorders is subtle and circuit-specific, most consistently affecting pathways linking posterior temporal and parietal regions rather than producing gross commissural malformations ref [14], ref [14], ref [16], ref [17], ref [18].

subsections.section_title: Concluding and Supplementary Material
subsections.subsection_title: Syndromic and Genetic Conditions
subsections.content:
Callosal involvement in genetic and syndromic neurodevelopmental disorders is heterogeneous, ranging from complete agenesis to subtler regional dysmorphology and microstructural disruption. A broad MRI survey across multiple malformation syndromes found corpus callosum abnormalities in roughly half of affected patients, often accompanied by white-matter alterations, underscoring that callosal pathology is not confined to a few canonical syndromes but may represent a recurrent marker of disturbed brain maturation in syndromology more generally [12].

Turner syndrome provides a clear example of this spectrum. Case reports have described complete agenesis of the corpus callosum, including in 45,X and ring-X mosaics, suggesting that severe callosal maldevelopment can occur in a subset of patients [1]. Beyond rare agenesis, morphometric MRI studies in Turner syndrome indicate more subtle midline abnormalities, including altered callosal morphology and reduced genu area, alongside posterior fossa changes, consistent with disrupted interhemispheric and broader midline development [11].

In Williams syndrome, several structural MRI studies have reported atypical callosal size and shape, although the direction of change can vary by subregion and analytic approach, implying nonuniform remodeling rather than a single stereotyped lesion [7]. In 22q11.2 deletion syndrome/velo-cardio-facial syndrome, quantitative MRI and DTI studies show both macrostructural and microstructural abnormalities involving the corpus callosum, particularly posterior and midline white matter, with broader alterations in connected association pathways [10, 8]. Together, these disorders illustrate that callosal findings can index distinct genetic mechanisms while converging on abnormal long-range connectivity, a theme relevant to the cognitive and behavioral phenotypes seen across syndromic developmental conditions [7, 8, 10, 12].

subsections.section_title: Concluding and Supplementary Material
subsections.subsection_title: Autism Spectrum Disorder
subsections.content:
Corpus callosum abnormalities are among the more reproducible neuroanatomical findings reported in autism spectrum disorder, although the exact topography varies across cohorts and methods. Early MRI studies described smaller total or regional callosal size, with reductions reported in posterior segments in some samples and in anterior regions in others, suggesting heterogeneity rather than a single uniform pattern ref [7], ref [6], ref [58].

This heterogeneity is illustrated by studies that controlled differently for age, IQ, and brain size. Piven et al. found smaller body and posterior callosal regions after adjustment for total brain volume, whereas Hardan et al., in high-functioning autism, emphasized reduced genu and rostral callosal area, particularly after accounting for intracranial and white-matter volumes ref [6], ref [58]. More refined regional analyses further suggested that head size matters: in normocephalic autism, genu and midbody reductions were evident, but these effects were attenuated in autistic individuals with macrocephaly, underscoring the importance of considering early brain overgrowth and scaling effects in ASD morphometry ref [59].

Diffusion-based work extends these morphometric findings by implicating altered microstructural integrity within and around the callosum. Developmental DTI studies reported lower fractional anisotropy in the posterior midbody/isthmus and in frontal callosal projections near the genu across adolescence and adulthood, with limited evidence for age-related normalization ref [67]. Together, these data support the view that ASD often involves atypical interhemispheric connectivity, but that callosal involvement is modest in magnitude, regionally variable, and shaped by developmental stage, cognitive level, and macrocephaly status rather than representing a unitary diagnostic signature ref [67], ref [59], ref [58], ref [6], ref [7].

subsections.section_title: Concluding and Supplementary Material
subsections.subsection_title: ADHD and Tourette Syndrome
subsections.content:
Findings in ADHD have implicated the corpus callosum primarily as a subtle, regionally selective rather than grossly malformed structure. Early morphometric MRI studies reported smaller posterior callosal regions, especially the splenium, in children with ADHD, with some reports also suggesting involvement of anterior sectors such as the genu or rostral body depending on the parcellation scheme and sample composition ref [68], ref [70], ref [56]. A meta-analytic review of pediatric studies concluded that the most reproducible alteration was reduced splenial size, while also emphasizing heterogeneity related to sex, comorbidity, and measurement method ref [55].

This structural variability is important in interpreting ADHD as a disorder of atypical interhemispheric integration rather than uniform callosal hypoplasia. Functional evidence supports this view: an event-related potential study of adults found abnormal directional asymmetry of interhemispheric transfer, with subtype-specific patterns—slower right-to-left transfer in inattentive ADHD and faster left-to-right transfer in combined ADHD—suggesting that callosal physiology may differ across clinical presentations even when gross anatomy is only modestly altered ref [56]. Together, these data are consistent with disrupted long-range coordination between frontal and posterior attentional systems, but they also caution against treating ADHD as a single callosal phenotype ref [55], ref [69].

Tourette syndrome provides a useful comparison because tic disorders frequently co-occur with ADHD yet may show a different callosal signature. Diffusion tensor imaging in boys with Tourette syndrome demonstrated reduced fractional anisotropy across all callosal subregions, indicating diminished white-matter connectivity even when midsagittal area differences were not prominent in that sample ref [69]. Earlier morphometric work had likewise reported reduced callosal area in Tourette syndrome, supporting the broader conclusion that developmental psychiatric disorders with attentional and motor-control symptoms can involve callosal abnormalities, although the affected metrics and inferred mechanisms may differ between ADHD and tic disorders ref [6], ref [69].

subsections.section_title: Concluding and Supplementary Material
subsections.subsection_title: Perinatal Risk, Prematurity, and Prenatal Exposure
subsections.content:
Perinatal adversity, especially very preterm birth, is consistently associated with altered callosal development. Quantitative MRI studies in school-age children and adolescents born very preterm or very low birth weight describe reduced total callosal area, with the most robust effects in posterior regions, and greater abnormalities in those with neonatal hemorrhage, ventricular dilatation, or other white-matter injury ref [49], ref [43], ref [8]. Importantly, smaller callosal size in preterm cohorts has been linked to poorer neuropsychological and motor outcomes, including weaker verbal skills, visuomotor integration, and motor coordination, again with notable sensitivity of posterior callosal sectors ref [49], ref [43], ref [46].

At the same time, the relation between structural abnormality and later school performance is not uniformly direct. In very low birth weight adolescents, qualitative MRI abnormalities—including callosal thinning—were common, yet broad school difficulties did not map cleanly onto lesion status alone, suggesting that diffuse developmental vulnerability and postnatal growth may contribute alongside focal perinatal injury ref [8]. Functional imaging nevertheless indicates that early callosal damage has lasting systems-level consequences: young adults born very preterm with callosal injury show altered activation patterns on tasks requiring interhemispheric transfer, consistent with compensatory reorganization rather than simple loss of function ref [46].

Prenatal toxic exposure provides a parallel developmental route to callosal dysmorphology. In fetal alcohol spectrum disorders, early morphometric work documented reduced callosal area and even agenesis in some heavily exposed children ref [50]. Later diffusion studies extended these findings, showing reduced fractional anisotropy and broader microstructural abnormalities in the splenium and other posterior callosal pathways, with correlations to visuomotor and related neurobehavioral deficits ref [47], ref [72]. Together, the prematurity and prenatal-exposure literatures emphasize that callosal involvement often reflects disruption of distributed white-matter maturation, with posterior callosal regions appearing especially vulnerable ref [49], ref [47], ref [72].

subsections.section_title: Concluding and Supplementary Material
subsections.subsection_title: Language, Reading, and Cognitive Correlates
subsections.content:
Language and literacy outcomes provide an important complementary lens on corpus callosum development because reading and phonological processing depend on efficient coordination across distributed bilateral networks. In children, diffusion properties of temporal callosal fibers have been linked to phonological awareness and related reading measures, with posterior/temporal callosal microstructure showing one of the clearest white-matter correlates of early reading skill ref [14]. More broadly, individual differences in anatomy have also been shown to predict oral-language and reading impairment, supporting the view that callosal metrics should be interpreted within larger language-network organization rather than as isolated morphologic findings.

The dyslexia literature has long implicated atypical callosal morphology, although the direction and locus of effects vary across cohorts and methods. Early MRI work reported larger splenial area and altered posterior asymmetry in dyslexic readers, consistent with abnormal interhemispheric organization involving temporo-parietal/angular regions ref [64]. Family-based MRI analyses later suggested that better readers within families had larger midsagittal callosal area, especially in the midbody, whereas total callosal volume was less informative than area measures ref [65]. Other studies have likewise described altered splenial or isthmic morphology in dyslexia, though not uniformly, underscoring phenotypic and methodological heterogeneity.

Beyond reading, cognitive correlates of callosal anomalies are evident in developmental callosal disorders themselves. Individuals with agenesis or dysgenesis often show relatively preserved basic language but weaknesses in higher-order inference, complex problem solving, social cognition, and processing speed, particularly when tasks require interhemispheric integration. Thus, across both idiopathic reading disorder and structural callosal malformation, the emerging theme is that callosal development modulates not only language acquisition and literacy, but also broader integrative cognitive efficiency ref [14], ref [64], ref [65].
